key_claims: Pakistan has provided the Taliban with military advisers, logistics, funding, arms transshipment and recruits despite official denials.

Saudi Arabia funded and subsidized fuel to the Taliban via Pakistan.
Iran and Russia support the United Front, with Russia enabling resupply and aid transport.
Arms continued to cross at Torkham in violation of UN sanctions imposed in December 2000.
The Six Plus Two group's pledges lacked enforcement, and several members violated them.
Pakistan is the Taliban's primary ally and key conduit of arms, ammunition and fuel, yet has publicly agreed to an embargo on both sides.
Six Plus Two members pledged in Tashkent not to arm Afghan parties but continued to supply them, fostering a culture of impunity.
UN sanctions on the Taliban target bin Laden and training camps but not abuses against civilians.
Supply routes for the Taliban from Pakistan are numerous and hard to monitor, unlike the United Front's.
HRW urges a comprehensive, enforced embargo on all parties with human rights benchmarks.
Fuel reaches the Taliban via two transshipment points from Pakistan and one from Turkmenistan.
The Taliban emerged from Deobandi madrasas in Afghanistan and Pakistan, including the JUI's Dar-al 'Ulum Haqqania headed by Samiul Haq.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia provided the military and financial resources that made the Taliban an effective force; an estimated 8-15,000 of its fighters are non-Afghans.
The Taliban's Ministry of Enforcement of Virtue and Suppression of Vice is arguably its most powerful agency and is reportedly Saudi-funded.

The United Front is a fractious coalition (Jamiat, Wahdat, Junbish, Harakat-i Islami, Ittihad-i Islami) in which each leader had different neighboring patrons, with Iran and Russia supporting Massoud and others.
Pakistan switched its favor from Hikmatyar's Hizb-i Islami to the Taliban in 1994, after which the Taliban captured Hikmatyar's heavy weapons in 1995.
The Taliban buys support of former mujahidin groups and defectors, including Hizb-i Islami-associated groups, Junbish commanders and Akbari's Wahdat faction.
HRW urges the UN to press Pakistan to comply with an arms embargo and accept monitors, as the fuel and arms supply reaches the Taliban via Pakistani transshipment points.

Pakistan backed the Taliban from about October 1994 to secure trade routes to Central Asia and install a friendly government in Kabul.
